name: Mongolia
traditionNote: A civil-law system rebuilt after 1990 on German and continental models over a Soviet-era institutional base: the enacted text governs, the codes are recent — a Civil Code of 2002 and a Criminal Code of 2015 — and courts do not bind one another by precedent, though the Supreme Court issues interpretations that are binding on lower courts.
summary: Laws (хууль) are passed by the State Great Khural, the single-chamber parliament enlarged to 126 members by the 2023 constitutional amendment, and are signed and promulgated by the President, who may veto a law or part of it — a veto the Khural overrides by a two-thirds majority. A law is officially published in Төрийн мэдээлэл, the State Information bulletin, and takes effect ten days after publication unless it fixes its own date. Below statutes sit the resolutions of the Khural and the Government, presidential decrees, and the administrative normative acts of ministries and agencies, which must be registered with the Ministry of Justice and published in their own compilation — an unregistered administrative act has no legal effect, which makes that register a real filter rather than a formality. Constitutional review is exercised by the Цэц, the Constitutional Court, in a two-stage procedure peculiar to Mongolia: the Court first issues a conclusion that a provision breaches the Constitution, the Khural may accept or reject it, and only if it is rejected does the Court decide finally and invalidate the provision.
hierarchy: Монгол Улсын Үндсэн хууль (Constitution of 1992, amended in 1999, 2000, 2019 and 2023)
International treaties to which Mongolia is a party, which under Article 10 become effective as domestic legislation on entry into force
Хууль — laws of the State Great Khural
Улсын Их Хурлын тогтоол and Ерөнхийлөгчийн зарлиг — resolutions of the Khural and decrees of the President
Засгийн газрын тогтоол — resolutions of the Government

gazette.name: Turiin medeelel
gazette.authority: Published under the Law on Legislation; issues hosted by the Хууль зүйн үндэсний хүрээлэн (National Legal Institute) in the unified legal information system
gazette.coverage: Issues by year and number from 1991 to the current year, with a small number of earlier items; the compilation of administrative normative acts is published alongside it in the same section
gazette.desc: The bulletin in which a Mongolian law is officially published and from which its entry into force is counted. It appears alongside a second compilation for administrative normative acts — the ministerial and agency rules that must be registered before they have effect — so the section holds both halves of the published corpus.
gazette.howto: Choose ТӨРИЙН МЭДЭЭЛЭЛ ЭМХЭТГЭЛ or ЗАХИРГААНЫ ХЭМ ХЭМЖЭЭНИЙ АКТЫН ЭМХЭТГЭЛ, then pick the year and the issue number; issues are served as documents rather than as a searchable text corpus, so for text you generally start from the consolidated act instead.
gazette.note: The default is ten days from publication to entry into force. Where a law names its own date, that date governs, and transitional laws frequently do.

constitution.name: Undsen huuli
constitution.authority: Adopted by the People's Great Khural on 13 January 1992; maintained in the unified legal information system
constitution.coverage: In force since 12 February 1992, amended in 1999 and 2000, substantially in 2019, and again in 2023 to enlarge the parliament and change the electoral system
constitution.desc: The constitution of the post-communist republic: a parliamentary system with a directly elected president holding a veto, a catalogue of rights, and in Article 10 a provision making treaties effective as domestic law once they enter into force. The 2019 amendment reworked the relationship between the president, the parliament and the government after nearly three decades of instability.
constitution.howto: Read the consolidated text in the legal information system, where the Constitution has its own category; the Constitutional Court publishes it alongside the acts governing its own procedure, and an English translation is in the system's English section.
constitution.note: Amendment requires a three-quarters majority of the State Great Khural, and the Constitution forbids amending it more than once in eight years on the same question.

sources.name: Legalinfo — unified legal information system
sources.authority: Хууль зүйн үндэсний хүрээлэн (National Legal Institute), under the Ministry of Justice
sources.coverage: Laws in force, with separate collections for repealed acts and for acts whose operation has been suspended; also Khural and Government resolutions, presidential decrees, treaties and Constitutional Court decisions
sources.desc: The state's single legal database, and in practice the only workable route into Mongolian law. Its categories are the constitutional hierarchy made navigable: laws, Khural resolutions, presidential decrees, government resolutions, treaties and constitutional decisions each have their own collection.
sources.howto: Browse the in-force collection alphabetically or search; the repealed collection at /mn/dislaw/27 and the suspended collection at /mn/overlaw/27 are separate, which matters because a search of the live collection alone will not tell you that an act was repealed. The advanced search filters by type, issuing body and date.
sources.note: Consolidated texts are maintained by the Institute from the published bulletin; where wording is contested, the Төрийн мэдээлэл issue is the published record.

sources.name: Government and presidential acts (Legalinfo)
sources.authority: Засгийн газар (Government) and the President; published through the legal information system
sources.coverage: Government resolutions in force, with presidential decrees in the neighbouring collection and Khural resolutions in another
sources.desc: Where much of the operative detail is. A Mongolian statute typically leaves implementation to a Government resolution, which approves the regulation, the procedure or the tariff as an annex — so the rule you need is often an annex to a resolution rather than a section of a law.
sources.howto: Browse the resolutions collection or search by number and year; annexes are part of the resolution document. Presidential decrees are at /mn/law/30 and Khural resolutions at /mn/law/28.
sources.note: Ministerial and agency rules are a separate category: they are administrative normative acts, and they must be registered with the Ministry of Justice and published in their own compilation before they bind anyone.

sources.name: Treaties (Legalinfo)
sources.authority: Хууль зүйн үндэсний хүрээлэн, publishing treaties ratified by the State Great Khural
sources.coverage: Treaties to which Mongolia is a party, in the same system as domestic legislation
sources.desc: Article 10 of the Constitution makes a treaty effective as domestic legislation once it enters into force for Mongolia, which puts treaties inside the operative corpus rather than beside it — and is why they sit in the same database as the statutes.
sources.howto: Browse or search the treaty collection by title or party; the ratifying law is a separate item in the laws collection and is worth reading for any reservation or implementing provision.

sources.name: Undsen huuliin tsets
sources.coverage: The Court's conclusions and decisions, the acts governing its jurisdiction and procedure, and its rules
sources.desc: A specialised constitutional tribunal of nine members outside the ordinary judiciary, reachable on the petition of a citizen as well as by state bodies. Its procedure is two-stage: a conclusion that a provision breaches the Constitution goes to the State Great Khural, and only if the Khural rejects it does the Court decide finally and invalidate the provision.
sources.howto: Read the decisions section for conclusions and final decisions; the site also publishes the Constitution and the two acts that govern the Court, which is where the standing rules and the procedure are set out. An English version of the site is available from the language switch.
sources.note: The Court's decisions are also collected in the legal information system at /mn/law/31, which is often the easier route when you already have a citation.

sources.name: Supreme Court of Mongolia
sources.coverage: The Court's judgments and rulings, its interpretations of statute, judicial statistics and the rules of the courts
sources.desc: The highest court in civil, criminal and administrative matters. Its official interpretations of how a statute is to be applied bind the lower courts — the nearest thing in Mongolian law to precedent, and a power exercised as a general instrument rather than case by case.
sources.howto: Take the interpretations and the resolutions of the full court for the general rulings, and the electronic case database for individual judgments; case files across the whole court system are searchable at shuukh.mn.
sources.note: An interpretation binds courts but is not itself legislation; it is published by the Court rather than in the State Information bulletin.

sources.name: Shuukh.mn
sources.native: Монгол Улсын шүүхийн шийдвэрийн цахим сан
sources.coverage: Decisions of the Supreme Court and of the appellate and first-instance courts of every aimag and district, searchable by court, case type and date
sources.desc: Mongolia publishes judgments across the whole court structure in one database, from the Supreme Court down to the soum and district courts — a wider public case-law collection than several far richer countries maintain.
sources.howto: Choose the court from the picker — Улсын дээд шүүх for the Supreme Court, then the aimag or district courts by name — and filter by case type and date; decisions are served as documents with the case number and the parties.
sources.note: Everything is in Mongolian Cyrillic, and the search rewards the exact court name; there is no English interface.

sources.name: State Great Khural
sources.coverage: Bills submitted and in progress, laws passed, standing committee work, plenary sittings and the record of oversight activity
sources.desc: The parliament's own site, and the route to a bill while it is still a bill. The submitted-bills section shows what has been introduced, by whom and where it stands, which is the only reliable way to see a change coming before it is published.
sources.howto: Follow 'Өргөн мэдүүлсэн төсөл' for submitted bills and 'Хууль' for laws passed; the legislative-process pages explain the stages a bill goes through. The English section is thinner than the Mongolian one.
sources.note: The 2023 constitutional amendment enlarged the Khural to 126 members and introduced a mixed electoral system from the 2024 election.

sources.name: Draft consultation (Legalinfo)
sources.authority: Хууль зүйн үндэсний хүрээлэн, for the ministries and the Khural
sources.coverage: Draft laws and draft Khural resolutions open for comment, and in a parallel section draft administrative normative acts
sources.desc: The consultation stage, run inside the same system that publishes the finished law. The second track, for draft administrative normative acts, is the more useful of the two in practice: those rules never pass through parliament, so this is the only point at which they are visible before publication.
sources.howto: Open the list of drafts under discussion, with the closing date for comments; the administrative-act track is at /mn/discussion?id=2. Comments are submitted through the site after registration.
sources.note: A draft is not law and often changes; nothing here is citable as a rule.

sources.name: Legalinfo (English)
sources.coverage: A translation database with a small number of laws, resolutions and administrative acts in English — a fraction of the Mongolian corpus
sources.desc: The state's own English collection, and honest about its scale: the front page counts the translated laws and resolutions in dozens rather than hundreds. It is nonetheless the only official English source, and it carries the Constitution.
sources.howto: Switch to EN and open the translation database; check whether the translation matches the current Mongolian text before relying on it, since translations are made once and rarely revised.
sources.note: Translations are unofficial. Only the Mongolian text has legal force, and investors' English versions of mining and investment law circulate in several competing translations.

sources.name: National Legal Institute
sources.authority: Хууль зүйн үндэсний хүрээлэн, under the Ministry of Justice
sources.coverage: Research reports, legal commentary, training material and the Institute's publications, alongside the legislation on legislating itself
sources.desc: The body that operates the legal information system, and Mongolia's main producer of published legal research. Its material on the Law on Legislation and the General Administrative Law is the clearest account of how Mongolian norms are supposed to be made and registered.
sources.howto: Browse the publications and research sections; the pages on the Law on Legislation and the General Administrative Law set out the drafting, registration and publication requirements that determine whether an act is valid.
sources.note: Research and commentary, not a source of law.

sources.name: National Human Rights Commission
sources.native: Монгол Улсын Хүний эрхийн Үндэсний Комисс
sources.en: National Human Rights Commission of Mongolia
sources.authority: Хүний эрхийн Үндэсний Комисс, reporting to the State Great Khural
sources.coverage: Annual status reports on human rights and freedoms in Mongolia, recommendations to state bodies, and complaint decisions
sources.desc: The Commission's annual report is submitted to the Khural and is the most systematic published account of how Mongolian law is applied in practice — detention conditions, labour rights, herders' land use, access to justice — as against how the statutes read.
sources.howto: Take the annual status report for the year in question and the recommendations issued to particular ministries; both are published in Mongolian, with a selection in English.
sources.note: Recommendations are not binding, though the Khural debates the annual report.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a law
findLaw.steps: Search the in-force collection of the legal information system by title or keyword and open the consolidated text. If nothing comes up, check the repealed collection and the suspended collection separately — a search of the live collection alone will not tell you that the act you are looking for was repealed.

findLaw.task: Read the law as officially published
findLaw.steps: Find the issue of Төрийн мэдээлэл for the relevant year and number in the compilations section; the publication date in that issue is what the ten-day period to entry into force runs from, unless the law fixes its own date.

findLaw.task: Find the rule below the statute
findLaw.steps: Look first among Government resolutions, where the regulation or procedure is usually an annex to the resolution. If it is a ministry or agency rule, it is an administrative normative act: check the compilation of administrative acts, and remember that an act not registered with the Ministry of Justice and published has no legal effect.
findLaw.source: Засгийн газрын тогтоол / Захиргааны хэм хэмжээний актын эмхэтгэл

findLaw.steps: Use the judicial decisions database, choosing the court from the picker — the Supreme Court, an aimag or capital appellate court, or a first-instance court — and filter by case type and date. The Supreme Court's binding interpretations are published separately on its own site.

findLaw.task: Check whether a provision has been held unconstitutional
findLaw.steps: Search the Constitutional Court's decisions, and read the two stages: a conclusion that a provision breaches the Constitution does not itself invalidate it — the Khural may accept or reject the conclusion, and only after a rejection does the Court's final decision remove the provision.

findLaw.task: Follow a bill or a draft regulation
findLaw.steps: For bills, use the submitted-bills section of the Khural's site. For rules that never go to parliament — the administrative normative acts — use the consultation track in the legal information system, which is usually the only public sight of them before publication.
findLaw.source: Улсын Их Хурал / Төсөлд санал өгөх

findLaw.steps: Check the English side of the legal information system, which holds the Constitution and a limited translation database. Coverage is thin, so for most statutes the Mongolian text is the only version; treat privately circulated English translations of mining, investment and tax law with care and check them against the Mongolian.

subnational: Mongolia is a unitary state divided into 21 aimags and the capital, and below them into soums and districts, each with an elected Citizens' Representatives Khural and a governor nominated by it and appointed from above. These khurals do not legislate: they take decisions within the powers granted by statute — local budgets, land allocation, local fees, licensing of some activities — and the governors issue orders. Their decisions are published by the aimag or city administration itself, and are not gathered in the national legal information system, so local rules generally have to be obtained from the local administration. The capital has a special legal status set out in a statute of its own, and Ulaanbaatar's rules on land, transport and construction are among the most consequential local instruments in the country. Herders' customary use of pasture is regulated by national law rather than by local enactment, which is a recurring point of friction rather than a settled arrangement.
caveats: The unified legal information system is the practical source for Mongolian law, and it separates acts in force, repealed acts and acts whose operation is suspended into different collections — searching one is not searching the corpus. Consolidated texts are maintained by the National Legal Institute from the published bulletin; the Төрийн мэдээлэл issue is the published record, and it is served as document images rather than as searchable text. Administrative normative acts of ministries and agencies bind only if they have been registered with the Ministry of Justice and published, so an unregistered rule circulating on an agency website is not law. A Constitutional Court conclusion is not the end of the matter: the parliament may reject it, and only the Court's subsequent final decision invalidates the provision. English coverage is very limited, the translations are unofficial and rarely revised, and competing private translations of investment and mining law are in circulation. Local rules are published locally and are largely absent from the national system.
